title: How to build a debris hut (emergency shelter from sticks and leaves)
asks: how to build a debris hut
how do i make a shelter out of sticks and leaves
emergency shelter with no tent and no tarp
how thick should the leaves be on a debris hut
survival shelter in the woods with no gear
how to bild a debri shelter
stuck overnight in the forest with no gear, how do I build a shelter, over
answer: First choose a safe site: free of dead trees that may fall, and free from the threat of avalanches, rockslides, mudslides and flash floods. Look for loose rocks, dead limbs or other material that could fall on the shelter.
Collect all the natural materials before you begin building: framework, covering, bedding and insulation.
Make a tripod with two short stakes and a long ridgepole, or place one end of a long ridgepole on top of a sturdy base.
Secure the ridgepole (the pole running the length of the shelter) with the tripod, or anchor it to a tree at about waist height.
Prop large sticks along both sides of the ridgepole to make a wedge-shaped ribbing. Make the ribbing wide enough to accommodate your body and steep enough to shed moisture.
Place finer sticks and brush crosswise on the ribbing. This latticework keeps the insulating material (grass, pine needles, leaves) from falling through into the sleeping area.
Add light, dry, soft debris over the ribbing until the insulating material is at least 3 feet thick. The thicker the better.
Place a 2-foot layer of insulating material inside the shelter.
At the entrance, pile insulating material that you can drag in from inside the shelter to close the entrance, or build a door.
Finally, add shingling material or branches on top of the debris layer, so the insulating material does not blow away in a storm.
The Army survival manual rates the debris hut as one of the best shelters for warmth and ease of construction, and says to build it when shelter is essential to survival.
warnings: Shelters made of natural materials usually take the most time and energy to build. Make camp early, so you have plenty of time.
Do not skip the insulation under you: at rest, a person loses as much as 80 percent of body heat to the ground.
Use the buddy system to watch each other for cold injury, and watch for signs of frostbite and hypothermia.
If there is a radio, use it to call for help. In a forest, prepare fires to attract search planes: smoke is better by day and flame is better at night.

For warmth and ease of construction, the debris hut is one of the best (see figure 6-13 on page 6-15). When shelter is essential to survival, build this shelter. To make a debris hut, use the following steps:
Step 1. Make a tripod with two short stakes and a long ridgepole or by placing one end of a long ridgepole on top of a sturdy base.
Step 2. Secure the ridgepole (pole running the length of the shelter) using the tripod method or by anchoring it to a tree at about waist height.
Step 3. Prop large sticks along both sides of the ridgepole to create a wedge-shaped ribbing effect. Ensure that the ribbing is wide enough to accommodate the body and steep enough to shed moisture.

Step 4. Place finer sticks and brush crosswise on the ribbing. These form a latticework that will keep the insulating material (grass, pine needles, and leaves) from falling through the ribbing into the sleeping area.
Step 5. Add light, dry, soft debris over the ribbing until the insulating material is at least 3 feet thick—the thicker the better.
Step 6. Place a 2-foot layer of insulating material inside the shelter.
Step 7. At the entrance, pile insulating material that can be dragged to the entrance from inside the shelter to close the entrance or build a door.
Step 8. Finally, add shingling material or branches on top of the debris layer to prevent the insulating material from blowing away in a storm.
